title: GPU runtime fallbacks and stability investigation
next_steps: Redwood: share CUDA graph repro + nvprof traces link

Redwood: propose fallback policy and quantization config by 2026-10-12
action_items: Jordan Lee: collect nvprof, nsight and kernel selection traces and upload to shared drive by 2026-10-12

summary: Deep dive on GPU runtime instability Atlas observed under mixed workloads. Focus on kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM path and vLLM-style paths, CUDA graph replay fragility, KV cache eviction interplay with batching, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to collect repro traces and run controlled pilot comparing quantized TRTexec vs vLLM builds; next steps include trace handoff and pilot kickoff.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Redwood CSM), Sophie Martin (Atlas Platform Eng), Diego Ruiz (Atlas ML Infra), Liam O'Connor (Atlas CTO), Priya Desai (Atlas Security)
Shared artifacts: quick repro (link: internal/redwood/cuda-graph-repro), pilot template (link: internal/redwood/pilot-atlas), security slide deck (link: redwood.com/sec-docs)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, should we do quick intros?
[00:10] Liam: yeah I'll be brief, CTO, overseeing infra and risk for model infra.
[00:15] Sophie: Sophie, platform eng, we run the GPU fleet and manage production inference pipelines.
[00:20] Diego: Diego, ML infra, mainly tuning runtimes and quant tests.
[00:25] Maya: great, Jordan is our SE who will take us through the kernel-level traces. Jordan, over to you.

[00:35] Jordan: cool thanks. we looked at the repro you sent, the main pattern is under mixed short+long sequences we see occasional p95 spikes and sometimes CUDA graph replay failures. those failures lead to a fallback which sometimes goes to a slower path and causes sustained latency increase.

[01:05] Sophie: yeah the weirdness is spikes persist even when GPU utilization isn't saturated. memory sometimes climbs then the kernel swap happens and latency jumps.

[01:30] Jordan: what I think is happening — and this is consistent with similar cases — is kernel selection oscillation. the runtime chooses a TensorRT-LLM optimized kernel for certain seq lengths, but when a longer request arrives it triggers a different kernel path, CUDA graph replay state changes, and kv cache prefetch patterns are thrown off. that prefetch/eviction interplay causes extra copies.

[01:58] Diego: can you clarify by "kv cache prefetch" — our impl uses a per-session KV cache with soft-eviction after 10k steps. we did increase prefetch to reduce cold-starts.

[02:18] Jordan: right, so prefetching is great for throughput, but with CUDA graphs the runtime can bake in assumptions about cache offsets. when eviction happens mid-replay, the graph replay may reference stale offsets or the kernel layout changes and the graph replay path fails, so the runtime falls back to an interpreter path or a slower cuBLAS path.

[02:45] Luna (Customer note): (inaudible)

[03:00] Maya: quick question — are you running TRT-LLM via our TRT exec path or using an external Triton/TensorRT integration?

[03:08] Sophie: we're using an internal Triton fronted flow; we experimented with Redwood's dedicated runtime earlier in a dev env but not in production.

[03:20] Jordan: that's important — integration differences matter. when TRT is managed inside our runtime we control graph capture/replay semantics and fallback heuristics; external Triton sometimes manages graphs differently.

[03:40] Diego: could you sketch the fallback policy you use? i.e. when cudagraph replay fails do you replay the capture or just re-run without graph?

[03:50] Jordan: in our runtime we try a fast fallback: invalidate the graph, evict the bad capture, and run an immediate non-graph path for that request. if the non-graph path is slower it might change request timing and cause cascading prefetch evictions. we've seen two modes: immediate slow path with short-lived latency spike, or repeated oscillation where subsequent requests keep toggling paths.

[04:20] Sophie: that resonates. we've seen the repeated oscillation and it's brutal because our SLO is p95 < 120ms and those cascades push p95 to 600ms briefly.

[04:40] Jordan: on top of that, quantization can change kernel selection. int8 kernels choose a different matrix multiply routine and sometimes a different tiling that is incompatible with the captured graph assumptions. so mixing quantized and fp16 variants increases the state space.

[05:10] Diego: we tried 8-bit dynamic quant with a bias correction, and latency improves for stable batches, but instability increases under bursty traffic.

[05:30] Maya: let's capture the concrete asks early: we want to understand if switching to Redwood-managed TRT-LLM path or using a vLLM-inspired path would be more stable for your workload; also how to set batching/eviction to avoid oscillation.

[05:50] Liam: cost matters too — if the TRT path requires special infra or bursts into multi-gpu then we need the size/cost tradeoff.

[06:12] Jordan: good point; TRT-LLM often gives better per-token cost because it uses fused kernels and int8 support, but if fallback oscillation causes repeated rework the effective cost goes up. vLLM-style paths (more interpreter-y) have fewer brittle graph captures and sometimes are more stable at p95, at the cost of higher steady-state token cost.

[06:45] Sophie: we'd prefer predictable p95 even if tail cost is higher; our downstream systems are sensitive.

[07:00] Jordan: ok then the path forward is: reproduce with your real request mix, run two controlled pilots — 1) TRT-managed path with conservative graph capture and extended eviction windows, 2) vLLM-like non-graph heavy path with larger batch safety nets. measure p50/p95/p99, token cost, and cache hit rate.

[07:30] Diego: what tuning knobs do you recommend for eviction and prefetch?

[07:40] Jordan: a few: increase soft-eviction TTL to avoid evicting during bursts; limit prefetch aggressiveness (reduce lookahead); use workload-aware batching so small sequences don't force capture with large sequences — i.e., route short requests to a low-latency lane and long requests to a throughput lane. we can suggest concrete numbers after we see your sequence histogram.

[08:15] Priya: on the security side we need to confirm KMS usage for on-prem keys and whether any of these traces include PII. will you need raw traces?

[08:28] Maya: we'll ask for redacted traces. Jordan: ideally we get nvprof/nvtx and the minimal capture needed (no payload tokens), plus anonymized sequence lengths and session ids.

[08:45] Sophie: we can do that, we'll redact content and leave trace IDs.

[09:00] Jordan: good. i'll also mention a subtle kernel selection bug we found in one customer case: if you enable a specialized fused attention kernel, under certain sequence length transitions the runtime chooses an alternate kernel with a different workspace layout; the capture assumes fixed workspace offsets and the mismatch causes replay asserts. the runtime should detect and invalidate capture earlier rather than letting it fail at replay. we've implemented heuristics that check "workspace compatibility" before replay.

[09:40] Diego: is there a perf penalty to checking compatibility?

[09:45] Jordan: trivial, it's a metadata compare. the heavier cost is if you invalidate too eagerly — you lose graph speedups. that's why heuristics need to be tuned to your distribution.

[10:05] Sophie: any suggestions on quantization mixes? we want int8 when we can.

[10:12] Jordan: run int8 in a single-lane cluster if possible; mixing int8 and fp16 on the same GPU increases kernel path divergence. you can run parallel lanes: a quant lane and an fp16 lane, route requests based on model/precision. That avoids on-the-fly kernel selection switches.

[10:35] Liam: sounds like more infra to manage though. is that something Redwood Dedicated handles?

[10:42] Maya: yes, Dedicated can provision lanes with pinned model variants and route by policy. for on-prem we can provide a template for lane config and the runtime will do the routing, but it does require some orchestration.

[11:00] Sophie: ok, the other weird thing — we see memory gossip across sessions; memory climbs slowly and then a GC event triggers. could that be from kernel workspace leaks?

[11:12] Jordan: possibly. leaks in workspace allocations or stale KV entries that weren't freed by eviction. nvprof traces + memstat over time will make that clear. also check for nvlink/peer copies when running multi-gpu; sometimes those transfers are misattributed.

[11:35] Diego: we're on NVLink-equipped nodes but single-GPU per worker currently.

[11:42] Jordan: okay that simplifies things.

[11:48] Maya: let's switch briefly to pilot plan logistics. we'll run a 2-week controlled pilot with a canary route for 10% traffic, two runtime variants (TRT-managed, vLLM-style), and a safety fallback to your current stack. we'll measure p50/p95/p99, cache hit rates, and token cost.

[12:15] Sophie: can Redwood host the pilot or do we need on-prem?

[12:20] Maya: we can start hosted (fast) to validate kernel/fallback behavior, but for full fidelity given your VPC/compliance you probably want the on-prem template. recommended approach: start hosted short run to validate tuning, then move to on-prem pilot.

[12:40] Priya: for on-prem we need SOC2 artifacts and HSM/KMS integration details.

[12:45] Anika: we'll share security pack and KMS integration doc; Maya will send the link after the call.

[13:00] Diego: regarding metrics, besides latency and cost, what do you want for cache telemetry?

[13:05] Jordan: per-session KV hit rate, eviction counts, prefetch counts, and graph invalidation events over time. also capture the sequence length distribution and the timestamped path chosen (graph vs non-graph) per request.

[13:25] Sophie: will you instrument nvtx ranges so we can correlate GPU kernels to request ids?

[13:30] Jordan: yes we will add nvtx markers; that's part of the repro snippet we asked for.

[13:45] Maya: wrapping up, can we recap action items?

[13:50] Sophie: i'll export traces and a 24h request histogram, redact payloads, provide by 2026-10-11.

[14:00] Diego: i'll run a quick local run with increased TTL on KV cache and reduced prefetch and share metrics by 2026-10-10.

[14:10] Jordan: i'll collect the nvprof/nsight traces and prepare the two-run pilot config (TRT conservative capture vs vLLM lane) and send by 2026-10-12.

[14:20] Maya: i'll send pilot template, security pack, and pricing.

[14:28] Liam: ok thanks. if the pilot looks good we'll schedule on-prem kickoff and a contract for Dedicated lanes.

[14:40] Maya: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll follow up in the next email with links and timelines.

[14:50] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words uncertain (e.g., "TRT exec", "tensorRT-llm" misheard as "tenserRT"), speaker overlap near 02:45, some technical acronyms may be slightly garbled.
